chunks: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the bird that is sent from a distant city which it had never seen at all, yet it comes [back].

He said: O Ibn Udhaafir! It comes to the home of its owner from thirty farsakhs based on its recognition and reckoning. But when [the distance] exceeds thirty farsakhs, it goes to its keepers with its sustenance.

key_terms.أرباب: Keepers/lords — those who provide food and care for the bird
key_terms.الطير: The bird — referring to homing birds/pigeons used for message delivery in early Islamic civilization
key_terms.حسب: Reckoning/calculation — the bird's natural navigational sense
key_terms.فرسخ: Farsakh (parasang) — a classical unit of distance, approximately 4–6 km; thirty farsakhs is roughly 120–180 km
key_terms.معرفة: Recognition/instinct — the bird's innate capacity to navigate and recognize its home location

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about the homing range of carrier birds?
ai.summary: Muhammad ibn Udhaafir questioned Imam al-Sadiq (AS) about the remarkable homing ability of carrier birds sent from unfamiliar distant cities. The Imam explained that a bird can navigate back to its owner's home from up to thirty farsakhs (approximately 120–180 km) through its natural faculties of recognition and instinctive reckoning. Beyond that range, the bird loses its homing orientation and gravitates instead toward those who provide it with food and care — reflecting an early Islamic understanding of avian navigation limits that has practical implications for the permissibility of relying on such birds.
word_analysis: its keepers/those who provide for it

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, form Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Khalid, from Muhammad Bin Ismail, from Muhammad Bin Uzafar who said, 
‘I asked Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> about the bird sent with a message from the remote city which it had never seen at all, so it comes’.

So heasws said: ‘O Ibn Uzafar! It would come to the house of its own from thirty Farsakhs (about 120 kilometers) upon its recognition and its reckoning. So when it exceeds upon thirty Farsakhs, it goes to its nourishes with its sustenance’.
en.sarwar: 1. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from Muhammad ibn ’Isma‘il from Muhammad ibn ‘ Adhafir who has said the following: “I once asked abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a bird which is set free in a faraway area and the bird has never seen it but it comes back.

He (the Imam) said, ‘O ibn ‘Udha’fir, birds can come to the house of its owner from a distance of thirty farsakh (90 miles) because of its knowledge and environment, but if it is more than thirty farsakh then the bird comes for the sustenance which is determined for it.’”
